body: Skin lesions are described by terms such as macule, papule, plaque, vesicle, bulla, pustule and wheal, and by histologic words such as hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis (retained nuclei in the stratum corneum), acanthosis (epidermal thickening) and spongiosis (intercellular edema). Inflammatory dermatoses include psoriasis, an immune-mediated disease with well-demarcated silvery plaques on extensor surfaces, parakeratosis, regular acanthosis, loss of the granular layer and neutrophil collections called Munro microabscesses, with a Koebner phenomenon and the Auspitz sign, and an association with arthritis. Atopic dermatitis is eczema with spongiosis in people with atopy. Lichen planus presents with pruritic, purple, polygonal papules with Wickham striae and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermal-epidermal junction, which is linked to hepatitis C. Acne arises from follicular obstruction and Cutibacterium acnes.

Blistering diseases are divided by the level of the split. Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune disease with IgG against desmoglein 3 in the epidermal desmosomes, producing flaccid intraepidermal bullae that rupture easily, a positive Nikolsky sign, mucosal involvement, and a fishnet immunofluorescence pattern; the split is suprabasal, creating a tombstone appearance. Bullous pemphigoid is autoimmune against hemidesmosomes (BP180 and BP230), with tense subepidermal blisters in older adults, no mucosal involvement and linear immunofluorescence along the basement membrane. Dermatitis herpetiformis is subepidermal with IgA at the papillary tips, in celiac disease. Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are severe drug reactions to sulfonamides, allopurinol, and anticonvulsants, with epidermal necrosis and mucosal erosions.

Infections include impetigo (Staphylococcus aureus or group A streptococci), warts from HPV, molluscum contagiosum with umbilicated papules, and dermatophyte infections diagnosed by potassium hydroxide preparation. Seborrheic keratosis is a common benign pigmented stuck-on lesion; the sudden eruption of many is the sign of Leser-Trelat and can suggest cancer.

Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer, from basal cells of the epidermis in sun-exposed skin, with a pearly papule with telangiectasias, palisading nuclei and a cleft, and it almost never metastasises. Squamous cell carcinoma arises from sun damage and actinic keratosis, with keratin pearls, and may metastasise, especially at the lip, in immunosuppressed patients and from chronic wounds. Melanoma is a malignant tumor of melanocytes, with risk factors of sun exposure, fair skin and many nevi, with the ABCDE rule (asymmetry, border, color, diameter, evolution). The most important prognostic factor is the Breslow thickness, the depth of invasion in millimetres, and the radial growth phase precedes the vertical growth phase. BRAF V600E is often present. Markers are S-100 and HMB-45. Kaposi sarcoma is HHV-8-associated vascular tumor in AIDS.
A worked example: an older patient with tense bullae on the thighs, no mucosal lesions, and linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane has bullous pemphigoid, so the blister roof stays intact.

lessons.title: Breast Pathology
body: A breast mass is evaluated by clinical examination, imaging and tissue sampling. Benign conditions are common. Fibrocystic changes are the most frequent cause of lumps in premenopausal women, with cysts, fibrosis, adenosis and apocrine metaplasia that fluctuate with the menstrual cycle; they carry no increased cancer risk unless proliferative disease with atypia is found. Fibroadenoma is the most common benign tumor in young women, a mobile, well-circumscribed, rubbery mass of stromal and glandular tissue that grows with estrogen. Phyllodes tumor has a leaf-like architecture with a cellular stroma and can be benign or malignant. Intraductal papilloma is the usual cause of bloody nipple discharge. Fat necrosis follows trauma and mimics cancer. Acute mastitis in lactation is usually from Staphylococcus aureus. Gynecomastia in men results from an estrogen to androgen imbalance, as in puberty, cirrhosis and Klinefelter syndrome.

Cancer risk factors reflect lifetime estrogen exposure and genetics: female sex, age, early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, obesity after menopause and prior chest radiation. Hereditary breast cancer from BRCA1 and BRCA2, which repair double-strand DNA breaks, is autosomal dominant with high risk of breast and ovarian cancer, and BRCA1 tumors are often triple-negative. TP53 and PTEN mutations are rarer causes. Atypical hyperplasia raises risk several-fold.

Carcinoma in situ means malignant cells within the duct that have not crossed the basement membrane. Ductal carcinoma in situ may show comedo necrosis with calcifications detected on mammography. Lobular carcinoma in situ is usually an incidental, often multifocal and bilateral finding, and it is a marker of increased risk. Paget disease of the nipple is an eczematous nipple change from carcinoma cells in the epidermis, nearly always with underlying ductal carcinoma. Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type, is the most frequent, giving a hard stellate mass with fixation and skin dimpling. Invasive lobular carcinoma is characterised by loss of E-cadherin, with single-file growth and a diffuse pattern that is hard to see on imaging, and it is often bilateral. Inflammatory carcinoma is dermal lymphatic invasion with an erythematous swollen breast with peau d'orange appearance, and it is not an infection. Medullary and mucinous types have a better prognosis.

Biomarkers guide therapy: estrogen and progesterone receptors predict response to endocrine treatments such as tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors, and HER2 amplification predicts benefit from trastuzumab. Triple-negative tumors lack all three and have the worst prognosis, with chemotherapy as the backbone of therapy. Prognosis depends most on stage, specifically the status of the axillary lymph nodes, and also on tumor size, grade and receptor status. Sentinel lymph node biopsy identifies the first draining node. Spread favours axillary nodes, bone, lung, liver and brain.

A worked example: a 45-year-old with a new firm mass and screening mammography calcifications has an invasive ductal carcinoma, ER positive and HER2 negative; the receptor profile points to endocrine therapy as part of treatment.

lessons.title: Female Reproductive Tract and Pregnancy
body: Cervical cancer is caused by persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, mainly types 16 and 18, with E6 and E7 inactivating p53 and RB. Squamous intraepithelial lesions arise at the transformation zone and progress through cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grades 1 to 3 to invasive carcinoma over years, which is why screening by cytology and HPV testing works, and vaccination prevents infection. Koilocytes with perinuclear halos are the cellular hallmark of HPV effect.

In the uterus, endometriosis is functioning endometrial tissue outside the uterus, giving cyclic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, infertility and ovarian chocolate cysts. Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue in the myometrium with a globally enlarged, tender uterus. Leiomyomas (fibroids) are the most common pelvic tumor, estrogen-sensitive, benign and monoclonal, with rare transformation to leiomyosarcoma. Endometrial hyperplasia follows unopposed estrogen from obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome, estrogen-secreting tumors and unopposed estrogen therapy, and may progress to endometrioid endometrial carcinoma, which presents with postmenopausal bleeding and has PTEN mutations. Type II serous carcinoma arises from atrophic endometrium with TP53 mutation and a worse prognosis.

Ovarian tumors are classified by cell of origin. Epithelial tumors are the most common malignant type: serous cystadenocarcinoma is the most common, associated with BRCA1 and BRCA2 and with psammoma bodies, and it presents late with ascites and a high CA-125; mucinous tumors can reach large sizes, and rupture can cause pseudomyxoma peritonei. Germ cell tumors affect young women: dysgerminoma resembles testicular seminoma, mature teratoma (dermoid cyst) is the most common benign ovarian tumor and may contain thyroid tissue (struma ovarii), yolk sac tumor secretes alpha-fetoprotein with Schiller-Duval bodies, and choriocarcinoma secretes hCG. Sex cord-stromal tumors include granulosa cell tumors with Call-Exner bodies, estrogen production and inhibin, and fibromas, with Meigs syndrome of ascites and pleural effusion. Polycystic ovary syndrome features anovulation, hyperandrogenism and insulin resistance.

In pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy is implantation outside the uterus, usually in the fallopian tube, with risk after pelvic inflammatory disease, and it presents with pain, bleeding and a positive pregnancy test and can rupture. Preeclampsia is hypertension with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks, from abnormal placentation with endothelial dysfunction, and eclampsia adds seizures; HELLP syndrome includes hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets, and delivery is the definitive treatment. Hydatidiform mole shows swollen chorionic villi and trophoblastic proliferation with a very high hCG; a complete mole is 46,XX from paternal chromosomes only with no fetal tissue, whereas a partial mole is triploid with fetal parts. Choriocarcinoma may follow a mole and metastasises to the lung and responds well to chemotherapy.
A worked example: a 28-year-old with amenorrhea, a very high hCG, vaginal bleeding and a snowstorm pattern on ultrasound has a complete hydatidiform mole.

lessons.title: Male Reproductive Tract and Prostate
body: Testicular germ cell tumors are the most common cancers in young men. Seminoma is the most common single type, with sheets of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and a fried-egg appearance, a lymphocytic infiltrate and a placental alkaline phosphatase marker, and it is highly radiosensitive and has an excellent prognosis. Embryonal carcinoma is more aggressive with glandular patterns. Yolk sac tumor is the most common testicular tumor in infants and secretes alpha-fetoprotein. Choriocarcinoma secretes hCG and may cause gynecomastia and early hematogenous spread. Teratoma contains tissue from multiple germ layers. Mixed tumors are frequent. Risk factors include cryptorchidism, which also impairs fertility, and orchiectomy is performed through an inguinal incision because a scrotal approach could alter lymphatic drainage. Testicular lymphatics drain to the para-aortic nodes, whereas scrotal skin drains to the inguinal nodes. Leydig cell tumors make androgens and Reinke crystals, and Sertoli cell tumors are rarer.

Other scrotal disorders include testicular torsion, which is a surgical emergency in adolescents with sudden pain, a high-riding testis and an absent cremasteric reflex, from twisting of the spermatic cord and venous infarction; epididymitis is infectious, with Chlamydia and gonorrhea in young men and coliform organisms in older men. Varicocele is dilation of the pampiniform plexus, more often on the left because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, and renal cell carcinoma invading the renal vein can cause it. Hydrocele is fluid in the tunica vaginalis, which transilluminates. Phimosis, balanitis and Peyronie disease affect the penis, and squamous cell carcinoma of the penis is linked to HPV and lack of circumcision.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a nodular hyperplasia of the periurethral transition zone from dihydrotestosterone, causing hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia and urinary retention, with bladder hypertrophy and hydronephrosis in severe cases; it is treated with alpha blockers, which relax smooth muscle, and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, which shrink the gland. Prostate cancer is mainly adenocarcinoma of the peripheral zone, which is why it may be felt on rectal examination, and is graded with the Gleason system, now converted to Grade Groups. It often grows slowly, and PSA is a screening tool with limits because it is organ specific and not cancer specific, and rises in BPH, prostatitis and after instrumentation; screening decisions are individualised and made with shared decision-making. Spread is to the bone as osteoblastic lesions in the axial skeleton through the vertebral venous plexus, and androgen deprivation is central to treatment of advanced disease. Acute prostatitis is usually E. coli.

A worked example: a 70-year-old with back pain and sclerotic vertebral lesions with a markedly raised PSA has metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma, and the sclerotic bone appearance marks osteoblastic activity.

questions.prompt: A person who has smoked for years has bronchial biopsy showing stratified squamous epithelium in place of ciliated columnar epithelium. What is this change?
choices: Hyperplasia, a reversible increase in the number of ciliated cells
Atrophy, a reversible loss of cell size from reduced workload
Metaplasia, a reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another
Dysplasia, a disordered growth that is already a carcinoma in situ

questions.prompt: Which change best explains why the myocardium thickens in long-standing systemic hypertension?
choices: Hyperplasia, as cardiac myocytes divide to increase their total number
Metaplasia, as myocytes are replaced by a more resistant cell type
Atrophy, as myocytes shrink and reduce the demand placed on the ventricle
Hypertrophy, as cardiac myocytes enlarge in response to pressure overload

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old man with 15 years of heartburn has an endoscopic biopsy showing intestinal-type columnar cells with goblet cells in the distal oesophagus. Which statement best describes the underlying process?
choices: Reprogramming of stem cells in response to chronic acid exposure, which leaves a field at risk of dysplasia and adenocarcinoma
Direct transformation of mature squamous cells into columnar cells, which carries no increased risk of later malignancy
Hyperplasia of the normal squamous lining caused by repeated cycles of healing, reversible only by surgery
Atrophy of the squamous lining followed by regeneration with identical squamous cells in a normal pattern

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old man presents 3 hours after chest pain begins. Cardiac myocytes are leaking intracellular proteins into the blood. Which finding best indicates that injury has become irreversible?
choices: Clumping of nuclear chromatin from falling intracellular pH
Profound membrane damage with irreversible mitochondrial dysfunction
Cellular swelling from failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump
Detachment of ribosomes from the endoplasmic reticulum

questions.prompt: Which sequence best explains why a hypoxic cell swells early?
choices: Less ATP stops protein synthesis, so osmotically active proteins build up inside
More lactate leaves the cell, so the cytoplasm becomes hypertonic to the outside
Less ATP slows the sodium pump, so sodium and water accumulate in the cell
More ATP drives the sodium pump too hard, so water is drawn into the cell

questions.prompt: Which pattern of necrosis is typical of an ischaemic infarct in the kidney?
choices: Fat necrosis, with chalky deposits formed from calcium soaps
Coagulative necrosis, with the tissue outline preserved for days
Liquefactive necrosis, with the tissue digested to a viscous fluid
Caseous necrosis, with granular debris inside a granulomatous rim

questions.prompt: A cell undergoing apoptosis releases cytochrome c from mitochondria. Which molecule is activated next in this pathway?
choices: Caspase 9, through formation of the apoptosome
Caspase 8, through recruitment by a death receptor
BCL2, through binding of the pro-apoptotic protein BAX
FasL, through cleavage at the cell surface by caspase 3

questions.prompt: A 40-year-old woman has a lymph node biopsy showing follicular lymphoma with t(14;18). Which mechanism most directly explains the survival of her tumor cells?
choices: Loss of caspase 8 so that death receptor signalling cannot proceed
Excess FasL on the tumor cells that kills attacking T lymphocytes
Increased BAX that opens the mitochondrial membrane to promote survival
Overexpression of BCL2 that prevents mitochondrial release of cytochrome c

questions.prompt: A 25-year-old woman is admitted after an intentional acetaminophen overdose. Transaminases are very high and biopsy shows necrosis around the central veins. Which is the best explanation for the distribution of injury?
choices: Zone 3 hepatocytes have the highest glutathione stores and are overwhelmed first
Zone 1 hepatocytes are the first to receive toxin from the portal vein and are lysed
Zone 3 hepatocytes have the highest cytochrome P450 activity and make the toxic metabolite
Zone 1 hepatocytes receive the most oxygen and so produce the most free radicals

questions.prompt: Why can an ischaemic tissue appear more damaged shortly after blood flow is restored?
choices: Returning oxygen blocks anaerobic glycolysis, so lactate falls too quickly
Returning oxygen generates a burst of free radicals and calcium overload
Returning blood flow washes out all of the stored cellular ATP at once
Returning blood flow causes immediate fibrinoid necrosis in vessel walls

questions.prompt: Which adhesion molecule family mediates the initial rolling of leukocytes along activated endothelium?
choices: Selectins, such as P-selectin and E-selectin
Integrins, such as LFA-1 binding to ICAM-1
Cadherins, such as VE-cadherin at cell junctions
Immunoglobulin superfamily members, such as PECAM-1

questions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes an exudate from a transudate?
choices: Low protein content due to decreased lymphatic drainage
High protein content due to increased vascular permeability
Low protein content due to increased hydrostatic pressure
High protein content due to decreased plasma oncotic pressure

questions.prompt: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent abscesses of lymph nodes and lung due to Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus. A dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry test shows no oxidative burst. Which defect is most likely?
choices: Myeloperoxidase deficiency, so hypochlorous acid is not generated
Complement C5b-9 deficiency, so bacteria cannot be lysed on the surface
NADPH oxidase deficiency, so phagocytes cannot generate superoxide
CD18 integrin deficiency, so neutrophils cannot adhere to the endothelium

questions.prompt: A 30-year-old woman has a chest radiograph with hilar lymphadenopathy. A lymph node biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. Which cell product is most important for activating the macrophages that form them?
choices: Interleukin 4 secreted by T-helper 2 lymphocytes
Histamine released by degranulating tissue mast cells
Complement C5a generated at the site of tissue injury
Interferon gamma secreted by T-helper 1 lymphocytes

questions.prompt: A child born with delayed separation of the umbilical cord, recurrent infections without pus and very high blood neutrophil counts most likely has which defect?
choices: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency from CD18 integrin mutations
Chronic granulomatous disease from NADPH oxidase mutations
Chediak-Higashi syndrome from a lysosomal trafficking protein defect
Selective IgA deficiency from impaired class switching of B cells

questions.prompt: Which type of tissue can regenerate after injury but is normally quiescent?
choices: Labile tissue, such as the intestinal mucosa
Permanent tissue, such as cardiac myocytes
Fibrous tissue, such as a mature scar
Stable tissue, such as hepatocytes

questions.prompt: Which cell is responsible for contraction of a healing skin wound?
choices: Endothelial cell forming the new capillary sprouts
Keratinocyte migrating across the granulation tissue
Myofibroblast containing smooth muscle actin
Neutrophil recruited by chemokines early in repair

questions.prompt: A 70-year-old malnourished man develops perifollicular haemorrhages, swollen bleeding gums and a surgical wound that has reopened. Which biochemical defect best explains the poor healing?
choices: Excess activity of matrix metalloproteinases, so collagen is degraded at the wound
Impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen, so it cannot cross-link
Impaired transcription of collagen genes, so fibroblasts cannot make procollagen
Failure of vitamin K-dependent carboxylation, so coagulation factors are not made

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old woman has a firm, raised scar that has grown well beyond the margins of her original ear-piercing site. Biopsy shows thick, glassy bundles of collagen. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: This is a keloid, and it extends beyond the original wound edges
This is a hypertrophic scar, and it stays within the original wound edges
This is granulation tissue, and it will remodel into a normal dermis
This is a fibrous dysplasia, and it is a type of benign bone tumor

questions.prompt: Which change drives the progression from chronic liver injury to cirrhosis?
choices: Apoptosis of hepatic stellate cells that normally store vitamin A
Replacement of hepatocytes by regenerating squamous epithelium
Increased degradation of type I collagen by hepatocyte proteases
Activation of hepatic stellate cells into collagen-producing myofibroblasts

questions.prompt: Which finding is typical of chronic right-sided heart failure?
choices: Hyperemia of the skin with warm, red, dilated arterioles
Hypoalbuminemia with generalised edema from urinary protein loss
Congestive hepatomegaly with a nutmeg appearance of the liver
Pulmonary hemosiderin-laden macrophages in the alveolar spaces

questions.prompt: A man with nephrotic syndrome develops periorbital and leg swelling. Which mechanism most directly explains the edema?
choices: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from right-sided failure
Obstruction of lymphatic drainage by tumor cells in the nodes
Increased endothelial permeability from circulating inflammatory cytokines
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from urinary albumin loss

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old woman with pneumonia and septic shock develops oozing from IV sites and bleeding gums. Labs show low platelets, prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen and a markedly raised D-dimer. Which mechanism best explains the bleeding?
choices: Widespread microthrombi consume platelets and clotting factors while fibrinolysis is activated
Production of an antibody directed against platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors
Failure to absorb vitamin K so that factors II, VII, IX and X are not carboxylated
Absence of von Willebrand factor so that platelets cannot adhere to damaged endothelium

questions.prompt: A 7-year-old boy has recurrent bleeding into the knee joints and a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT, platelet count and bleeding time. Which explains the pattern of bleeding?
choices: An antibody to platelet factor 4 causes platelet activation and thrombosis with thrombocytopenia
A deficiency of an intrinsic pathway factor impairs generation of thrombin on the platelet plug
A defect of platelet glycoprotein Ib impairs adhesion to subendothelial von Willebrand factor
A deficiency of protein C allows unchecked thrombin generation and consumption of factors

questions.prompt: Which test result most directly reflects plasmin degradation of cross-linked fibrin?
choices: A prolonged bleeding time
A reduced platelet count
An elevated D-dimer
A prolonged prothrombin time

questions.prompt: Which element of Virchow triad is the main driver of thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage during atrial fibrillation?
choices: Turbulence from a stenotic aortic valve
Abnormal blood flow, with stasis
Endothelial injury from rupture of a plaque
Hypercoagulability from a factor mutation

questions.prompt: Which feature of a thrombus indicates that it formed in flowing blood before death?
choices: Alternating pale and dark layers called lines of Zahn
A soft, gelatinous consistency with a yellow supernatant
A uniformly dark red colour with a smooth shiny surface
A loose attachment with no adherence to the vessel wall

questions.prompt: A 34-year-old woman 3 weeks after a long-haul flight and on oral contraceptives has sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. CT shows a saddle embolus. Her father had a similar event at a young age. Which inherited abnormality is the most common cause of this family history?
choices: Antithrombin deficiency causing loss of inhibition of factor Xa and thrombin
Deficiency of von Willebrand factor causing failure of platelet adhesion
Deficiency of factor VIII causing failure of the intrinsic coagulation pathway
Factor V Leiden mutation causing resistance to inactivation by activated protein C

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old man has a femur fracture. Two days after surgery he develops hypoxia, confusion and a petechial rash over the chest. Which type of embolus is most likely?
choices: Air embolus entering through a central venous line
Amniotic fluid embolus entering the maternal circulation
Fat embolus from marrow released at the fracture site
Thromboembolus from a deep vein of the calf

questions.prompt: Why do small pulmonary emboli rarely cause pulmonary infarction in a healthy person?
choices: The lung has venous drainage that reverses flow to bring blood to the area
The lung has a dual blood supply from the pulmonary and bronchial arteries
The lung has end arteries that tolerate occlusion without necrosis
The lung has a low oxygen demand and can survive without perfusion

questions.prompt: Which category of protein is most often affected in autosomal recessive disorders?
choices: Enzymes, because a heterozygote keeps enough activity to be healthy
Structural proteins, because half the amount is enough to be healthy
Receptor proteins, because half the number is enough to be healthy
Transcription factors, because half the dose is enough to be healthy

questions.prompt: A man with an X-linked recessive disease has children with a woman who is not a carrier. What is the outcome for their children?
choices: No daughters are carriers and all sons are affected
All daughters are carriers and no sons are affected
Half of the daughters are carriers and all sons are affected
All sons are carriers and no daughters are affected

questions.prompt: A 17-year-old tall, thin boy has arachnodactyly, a high arched palate, and upward lens dislocation. He is at greatest risk of which life-threatening complication?
choices: Coarctation of the aorta leading to hypertension
Aortic valve stenosis leading to syncope
Aortic root dilation leading to dissection
Mitral stenosis leading to atrial thrombosis

questions.prompt: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent Pseudomonas pneumonia, greasy foul stools and poor weight gain. A sweat chloride test is high. Which mechanism most directly explains his lung disease?
choices: Defective alpha-1 antitrypsin leads to unopposed elastase and alveolar destruction
Defective ciliary dynein leads to immotile cilia and impaired mucociliary movement
Defective NADPH oxidase leads to failure of neutrophil killing of catalase-positive organisms
Defective chloride secretion produces dehydrated, thick mucus that impairs clearance

questions.prompt: Two unaffected parents have a child with autosomal recessive disease. What is the chance that their next child is affected?
choices: 25 percent
50 percent
75 percent
100 percent

questions.prompt: Which trinucleotide repeat expansion causes fragile X syndrome?
choices: CAG repeats in HTT
CTG repeats in DMPK
GAA repeats in frataxin
CGG repeats in FMR1

questions.prompt: A child inherits both copies of chromosome 15 from the mother. What disorder results?
choices: Fragile X syndrome through methylation of the maternal alleles
Turner syndrome through loss of the paternal sex chromosome
Prader-Willi syndrome through loss of the paternal contribution
Angelman syndrome through loss of the paternal contribution

questions.prompt: A 15-year-old girl has short stature, a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples and primary amenorrhea. Which cardiovascular lesion is most likely?
choices: Persistent truncus arteriosus with a single arterial vessel
Bicuspid aortic valve or coarctation of the aorta
Atrioventricular septal defect with a complete common valve
Tetralogy of Fallot with right ventricular outflow obstruction

questions.prompt: A 9-month-old boy has developmental regression, an exaggerated startle response, a cherry-red macula and no hepatosplenomegaly. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
choices: Hexosaminidase A
Glucocerebrosidase
Sphingomyelinase
